title: Did Highways Cause Suburbanization?
research_question: To what extent did the construction of new limited-access urban highways contribute to the decline of central city populations in U.S. metropolitan areas during the second half of the twentieth century? How much of the observed central city depopulation, despite overall metropolitan growth, can be attributed to improvements in commuting infrastructure rather than to other drivers of suburbanization such as Tiebout sorting, racial composition changes, crime, or school desegregation?
data_description: The unit of observation is the U.S. metropolitan area (MSA), with MSA boundaries fixed at their 2000 definitions. The primary sample consists of 139 MSAs with at least 100,000 residents and central cities of at least 50,000 in 1950; a more selective sample restricts to 100 inland MSAs (central cities at least 20 miles from a coast, major lakeshore, or international border). Decennial data from 1950 to 1990 are drawn from the County and City Data Books, U.S. Censuses of Population and Housing, and 1950–1990 PUMS. Key variables include central city population (using both political and constant 1950 geography boundaries reconstructed from census tracts), MSA population, central city radius/area, simulated mean log income and Gini coefficients built from 1940 industry employment shares and national skill prices, and weather controls. Highway data come from the FHWA's PR-511 database combined with digital interstate maps and a 1947 national interstate highway plan, used to construct counts of highway 'rays' (segments passing within one mile of the CBD) for each MSA-year.
institutional_context: The setting is the planning and construction of the U.S. Interstate Highway System between 1950 and 1990. Federal involvement began with the Federal Aid Highway Act of 1944, which directed the roads commissioner to design a national network connecting principal metropolitan areas, industrial centers, and national defense sites, with routes 'as direct as practicable' rather than to serve local commuting. Following negotiations between states and federal authorities, a 37,324-mile national plan was approved in 1947, drawing on considerations of population, manufacturing, agriculture, military installations, and a 1941 War Department strategic network. Substantial federal funding only arrived with the 1956 Federal Aid Highway and Highway Revenue Acts, which expanded the system to 41,000 miles and committed 90% federal cost-sharing. Between 1950 and 1990, interstate mileage grew from 341 to 43,420 miles nationally, and from 161 to 16,716 miles within the sample MSAs, with most of the 1947 plan eventually built. State and local governments also funded additional urban expressways, suggesting that actual local highway construction responded partly to local commuting demand even as the planned backbone was designed for interregional purposes.
